To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the dimer evaporation rate constant for H2SO4 is in the range (2.0–2.9) × 10−10 cm3 s−1 for the temperature range 208–223 K and (ii) the formation of H 2SO4· NH3 is an essential step in dimer formation in the binary system.

we have measured the dimer evaporation rate of sulfuric acid for the first time in the free tropospheric temperature range, we have estimated the thermodynamic properties of H2SO 4·NH3 using our measurements, and we have measured large sulfuric acid clusters in the binary system for the first time.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the thermodynamic properties of the H2O–H2SO4 and H2O–NH4–H2SO3 systems.
the formation of sulfur-containing molecules and clusters in the gas phase.
the thermodynamics of clusters in the binary (sulfuric acid–water) and the ternary (sulfur dioxide–ammonia–water) system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formation of sulfur trioxide dimers is not a significant pathway to the formation of sulfur acid dimers in either the binary or ternary system.
the dimer evaporation rate of sulfuric acid at low temperatures can be described using a simple Arrhenius expression with a temperature-dependent activation energy.

sulfuric acid is a very efficient nucleating molecule, and the formation of dimers in the gas phase is the rate-determining step in the binary system, while in the ternary system H2SO4 and H2SO4NH3 clusters form in a very rapid equilibrium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thermodynamic properties of the H2S4·H2O dimer are well constrained for temperatures from 208 K to 248 K and that H2SO4 dimers are formed in the presence of ammonia.
we have shown that sulfuric acid dimmer formation in the binary and ternary system can be described using the same thermodynamic model.
the thermodynamic data for sulfuric acid dimer formation in both the binary and ternary systems are in good agreement with previously published results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dimer formation in both systems is thermodynamically favored over a wide range atmospheric conditions.
the formation of sulfur trioxide is not required for the formation of dimers and larger clusters of sulfuric acid.
the thermodynamics for the formation of sulfuratic acid clusters are now well constrained over a wide range (208–248 K) of atmospheric temperatures.
